institutionName: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: As a dramatic as possible culture change - and the weather!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The Greek school-system can be a bit heavy, especially when you are used to clear information e.g. about deadlines and other important information from the Danish system. It flows a bit more casual.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy! Once the semester started - before that, just forget about it. Don't waste time on too much research beforehand, it will just complicate things. The Erasmus Office at Panteion was VERY helpful and always available!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had a lot of questions, especially in the cource-selection period. I send A LOT of emails with Evie, the contact for Erasmus, and she was ALWAYS kind and helpful - I also dropped by her office some times.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I had a few options to choose from! I started the proces many months before. There are a lot of options available, but it takes some time. I used Facebook! Joined different Athens housing groups, and also check marketplace! There are both private landlords, and then there are a lot of people from companies that manege housing for Erasmus-like students. Ask about the rules for the contract in advance - some of these places has crazy rules about things like having visitors over.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I don't really think you can live on campus - living of is great! Don't ever count on buses as your best connection to school - they will come, but they can be very late, and due to traffic they are always much much later than expected. The metro is wonderful. I lived further from the metro, but still just 15 minutes walking. The only issues was that with big demonstrations or strikes happening, which happens a few times, especially Syntagma and Panepistimio can close down. But I didn't miss anything important.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Very easy, they have a Welcome day with a presentation, and then you just book an appointment online. You have to print out in advance the form from Mobility Online, but this is also very easy - there are copy-shops all over Athens, and it is very, very cheap to print.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinator was always available to answer my email, usually within a few days.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Oh this took a while.... I think other people has a more smooth experience than me. I wanted to make good use of my free selection of courses, so I chose a lot of different courses, but getting confirmation from the professors did not always happen so fast. Almost the whole first month the process is that you can try out courses, and then lock them in later. I locked down my final courses only in December, which was very late, but I cleared it with the Erasmus office at Panteion. The problem was that I needed to hit between 30 and 32 ECTS due to my university in DK, and the courses in Panteion was often very small, so I ended up with 6 courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't do too much research before the semester starts!! You never know what subjects from last year will be available to Erasmus. But apply for your Erasmus grant as early as possible, so you don't go without money, if the registration process drags out. Use the Erasmus course selection (different from the one available to Greek students - find it through the Panteion's Erasmus webpage), to apply for the grant. Then forget about the courses, and just wait for the new course-catalog. It will be published pretty late, when the semester starts - but this is okay! Because you have the whole first month to try out and select courses. Be aware that there is often no link between the number of ECTS and the exam that you have to perform - some 3 ECTS courses have giant exams, and some bigger have smaller. Just try to get that information, because you will start making your exams almost immediatly.

Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took a lot of courses outside of my normal field - so I don't really know.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is a lot of smaller classes, especially for Erasmus, because there is a lot of courses which is only for Erasmus, and not for Greek students. I took a lot of courses as reading courses. From the descriptions I thought I would be provided with bibliography that I would have to self-study - in most instances however, I was just provided with an exam description, and I had to find my own information, and basically just start writing my exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Key Issues in Psychology I
Language and Communication in Digital Media
Criminological approaches to Criminal Law and the Institutions of Criminal Justice Ι
Anthropology of Dance
Behavioural Analysis 
Statistics II

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Key Issues in Psychology I is an introduction course - the exam is just compulsory attendance. They introduce the other psychology courses that are available for Erasmus, I found it exiting and that is how I found Behavioural Analysis, which was exiting, and consisted of a good book that I was provided, and a handwritten exam. Statistics II was also good, provided material and multiple choice exam. I also liked Anthropology of Dance, but it was also a bit strange introduction-like course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not really any.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is cheap compared to DK - I spend more than I would in DK, but that was because I never cooked meals myself. Panteion has a canteen where Erasmus students can collect three meals per day also. Transport is super cheap for students, unlimited for 13 euro per month with Athena card, and even without transport is 1,20 euros for 90 minutes in the whole Athens area just by scanning your bank card. Computer and electronic repair is suuuuper cheap! My computer died COMPLETELY, and I had it fixed for 40 euros around Omonia.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Panteion has a lot of offers, Yoga, tennis, dance etc. I found my own activities outside of it, because I was a bit far from the university.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Erasmus student network have a lot of events, trips, parties, local events. I didn't attend.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend joining a local volunteer organisation! It is a good way to connect outside of University. I worked with street cats. The organisations Nine Lives and The Adespota Exarchia. They always need help with fostering or feeding cats. Had a beautiful feeding route one day a week in Zappeion garden. There are thousands of street-cats in Athens.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Voula is the best beaches, 1,5 hours from Athens! The Islands are of course also amazing. I stayed in Athens a lot - it is a city of endless things to do. Lycabettus Hill has the best view inside the city, and it is easy to walk, with a cafe on top. Try to catch a show at the Odeon of Herodes Atticus! It is ancient an a cool experience - both opera and dance-shows. The Eleonas market on Saturdays and Sundays, they sell every used item you can imagine. Also the 1-5 euro used clothes shops, mainly located in Omonia on Pattisia, called things like Italy Outlet. Local farmers markets on Saturdays on different streets.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, time is MUCH more relaxed in Athens - and I love it. Remember to tip service providers and restaurants! A lot of people know English, even though they say they don't.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I found it difficult, because the classes are so separate. I mostly socialized outside of the University.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Also the time understanding - especially when dealing with deadlines at my own university. But it ended up not really being a problem at all.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The relaxed time, the social life on the streets - Greeks are outside at cafes and bars every evening, every day of the week at all seasons. It is wonderfully vibrant!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Calm down <3 It may seem to move slow, but it is suppose to - lean into it, nothing bad will happen!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Hmmm, I think I covered it in the previous sections.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Helping the local girls with the cats!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I arrived early, and it took me a bit of time to meet people.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
